planting.note: Mount bare-root on cork bark, driftwood, or in a mesh basket with no soil; grow in bright indirect light and soak or mist regularly, shaking off standing water so the dense leaf base can dry within a few hours.

directions: This miniature Brazilian species is prized for its dense rosette of narrow, silvery, heavily scaled leaves that curl slightly inward, giving even a solitary head real presence in a small mounted display. Before blooming, the leaf bases and outer bracts flush deep rose to red while slender violet flowers emerge from the center, and the color intensifies with brighter light. Keep it mounted rather than potted, water by soaking or heavy misting two to three times a week, and ensure good airflow so the tightly packed leaf bases never stay wet overnight. Clumps form slowly from basal pups after flowering, eventually producing an attractive multi-headed specimen.

planting.note: Mount bare-root on cork bark or lava rock, or set loose in a shallow dish with other small air plants; give strong indirect to a few hours of gentle direct sun, and soak or mist two to three times weekly, drying fully between waterings.

directions: Native to dry montane scrub in Salta Province, northern Argentina, this compact species forms narrow, grayish-green leaves on a plant that is more often grown for its flower than its foliage. A single vivid red-orange tubular bloom emerges from the leaf axils in spring, sized disproportionately large for such a small plant and lasting for several weeks. It tolerates brighter, drier conditions than many soft-leaved Tillandsia and resents being kept constantly damp. Mature plants slowly produce basal offsets, eventually forming a small cluster of rosettes that bloom in succession.

planting.note: Mount bare-root on cork bark or driftwood in a cluster to encourage its natural clumping habit; grow in bright indirect light with regular misting or soaking, and allow the fine foliage to dry fully between waterings.

directions: This Bolivia-native species forms low, tight mounds of slender, finely scaled silvery-green leaves that make it look more like a cushion of foliage than individual rosettes. Small lavender-purple flowers appear in spring nestled among the leaf tips and are pleasantly fragrant, a trait not shared by many of its relatives. It clumps readily and quickly, making it a good choice for covering a mount or wreath form with a dense mat of texture. Give it the same bright light and dry-between-waterings routine as other fine-leaved Tillandsia species to avoid rot in its congested growth habit.

planting.note: Mount bare-root on cork bark or wire in a spot with excellent airflow; the dense woolly leaf covering holds water longer than smoother species, so mist lightly and more often rather than soaking, and favor bright light to keep growth compact.

directions: Native to dry oak and pine forests in Mexico, this species is grown almost entirely for its remarkable texture: slender leaves covered in a thick coat of fine silvery-white trichomes give the whole plant a soft, feathery, almost mossy appearance. It clumps into an airy, rounded mound over time and sends up short spikes of small purple flowers tucked among the fuzzy foliage. Because its dense covering of hairs slows evaporation, it is more prone to rot than smooth-leaved species if soaked and left damp, so favor frequent light misting over dunking and keep air circulating well around the mount.

planting.note: Mount bare-root on cork bark or driftwood; grow in bright indirect to gentle direct light and mist or soak regularly, favoring quick drying since the soft, densely haired leaves can rot if left wet.

directions: Found from southern Mexico into El Salvador, Honduras, and Nicaragua, this species forms a soft, silvery, finely haired rosette reminiscent of the popular Tillandsia tectorum but noticeably smaller and quicker to clump. The thin, slightly curling leaves give plants a fuzzy, almost snowball-like look that stands out among smoother air plants. Small tubular white to pale lavender flowers are tucked low in the rosette and easy to miss compared with the foliage display. It offsets freely from the base, forming an attractive multi-headed mound within a couple of years under good light and regular watering.

planting.note: Mount bare-root on cork bark or driftwood, or group several heads in a small dish; grow in bright indirect light and mist or soak two to three times weekly, letting the thin foliage dry fully between waterings.

directions: Ranging from Mexico south into Costa Rica, this species forms slender clusters of thread-fine, grass-like leaves that give it a much softer, grassier texture than most clump-forming air plants. It offsets quickly and densely from the base, filling out into an attractive tuft within a season or two under regular care. Small lavender to purple flowers appear at the leaf tips in spring, easy to overlook against the fine foliage. Its thin leaves dry out faster than fleshier species, so it benefits from slightly more frequent misting than thicker-leaved Tillandsia to avoid the tips browning.

planting.note: Mount bare-root in a dense cluster on cork bark or wire to show off its tangled, wiry habit; grow in bright indirect to gentle direct light and mist or soak regularly, letting it dry within a few hours each time.

directions: Native to open, dry scrub across Argentina, Bolivia, Paraguay, and Brazil, this species forms dense, tangled clumps of extremely fine, wiry, silvery-gray leaves that give mature plants a distinctive ball-like or shaggy appearance unlike almost any other air plant. Small lavender flowers appear tucked among the thin foliage in the warmer months. It is an unusually tough, drought-resistant species in its native grassland habitat, so it tolerates brighter light and longer dry spells than soft-leaved Tillandsia, but still grows and clumps fastest with regular misting or soaking.

planting.note: Divide offsets or pot up leaf-pulling plantlets into a mineral-rich, peat-and-perlite mix kept evenly moist through the growing season and allowed to stay only lightly damp through the dry-season rosette's winter rest.

directions: Endemic to damp limestone banks and cliffs in the Mexican states of Morelos, Guerrero, and Oaxaca, this butterwort produces two distinct leaf forms through the year: a flat, sticky-glandular summer rosette that actively traps gnats and small flies, and a tighter, smaller, succulent non-carnivorous rosette that carries it through its drier winter rest, a seasonal dimorphism shared with several other Mexican Pinguicula. Pale lilac to purple flowers with a paler throat rise on thin stalks above the foliage during the growing season. Grow it like other Mexican butterworts, in a mineral-rich, fast-draining mix with bright indirect light, and reduce watering noticeably once the compact winter rosette forms.

planting.note: Tuck divisions into the water-filled leaf tanks of a live tank bromeliad, or pot into pure wet sphagnum kept standing in rain or distilled water in a warm, humid, partially shaded greenhouse or terrarium.

directions: Native to the tepui highlands of Venezuela, Guyana, and northern Brazil, this remarkable bladderwort lives almost entirely inside the water-filled leaf reservoirs of giant tank bromeliads (Brocchinia species), sending out stolons that travel across wet rock or bark to find a new bromeliad tank to colonize. It carries the largest flowers and reportedly the largest underground bladder traps found anywhere in the genus, with tall stalks bearing showy lavender-purple blooms that can appear at almost any time of year. In cultivation it is grown mounted inside a live tank bromeliad or in a pot of pure sphagnum kept standing in acid, mineral-free water, and it needs constant humidity and warmth to thrive.

planting.note: Mount divisions on damp, mossy cork bark or pot into a fine peat-perlite mix kept constantly moist in bright, humid, partially shaded conditions, mimicking its habit of growing on wet rock faces and tree trunks in cloud forest.

directions: Widespread across the Antilles and northern South America (Brazil, Colombia, Guyana, Venezuela), this bladderwort grows as a terrestrial or epiphytic plant on wet, mossy rock faces and tree trunks in humid montane forest. Its thin stolons carry small underground tubers that help it survive drier spells, while thread-fine foliage bears the inconspicuous bladder traps typical of the genus. Tall, wiry flower stalks rise well above the foliage and carry large, showy orchid-like blooms in shades of white to pale lavender, among the showiest flowers in the genus. Keep it evenly moist in a bright, humid setting such as a terrarium or greenhouse, using only rain or distilled water.

planting.note: Press small divisions or sod pieces onto the surface of a wet peat-sand or peat-perlite mix and keep the tray shallowly flooded with rain or distilled water in bright, humid conditions such as a terrarium.

directions: Native to wet grassland and seepage areas in Argentina, Brazil, and Uruguay, this small terrestrial bladderwort forms a low, spreading mat of fine stems studded with microscopic underground bladder traps that capture soil-dwelling microorganisms. It is popular with terrarium and vivarium growers for its near-continuous production of small white flowers with a yellow throat marking, held just above the foliage on thin stalks. Keep it in a shallow tray of wet, nutrient-poor peat-based mix under bright indirect light or grow lights, watering only with rain or distilled water, and it will spread steadily to fill a pot or terrarium floor.
